[Headline:]
'Four Financial News [reporters?] settle EEO cases pursued by Guild since 1988'

[Body:]
'This month, four financial news reporters received substantial settlements from The Post to resolve their claims of discrimination filed under the 1997 Settlement Agreement of the Washington-Baltimore Newspaper Guild's 1988 charge of discrimination by The Post at the D.C. Office of Human Rights and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The terms of the settlements are subject to confidentiality agreements. The four reporters expressed their satisfaction with the settlements and thanked the Guild for its persistence in pursuing the cases.

The Guild's 1988 charge of race and gender discrimination at The Post was settled in 1997 by an EEOC-approved agreement that provided Post employees with a mechanism to pursue individual claims of discrimination. Eighteen such claims were filed. The above cases are among the last to be settled.'

[Subhead:]
'Keeping 'em honest'

documents.title: Compiled employee survey responses on race and gender at The Post (metoo/seniority quotes)
documents.subject: Typed compilation of Washington Post employees' own words (identified by race, gender, and desk) responding to questions about hiring, promotion, and AMEs — responses to a Guild/union survey on discrimination
documents.date: unknown (context suggests late 1990s, likely tied to the 1988 EEO charge / 1997 Settlement Agreement era)
documents.notes: Single typed page, two columns, ending mid-sentence at the bottom ('I don't think there is a commitment to minority hiring'). Appears to be one page of a longer compiled exhibit of unit members' survey answers attributed to 'Unit member'-style attributions.

pages.transcript:
[Left column:]
'Black female, Metro Reporter:
The questions are poorly phrased so as to be narrow in scope, so that the real point is being missed. It is clear by the behavior of upper management that there has been no genuine interest in recruiting blacks or Hispanics. The glaring examples are that there are only two on Style and two on National.
When blacks are hired they tend to be hired in the lowest position in Metro with little or no effort made to bring in senior reporters, editors or managers who might be able to strengthen editorial or newsroom policy.
One of the most significant problems with management at The Post is their blinding avoidance of helping new or low level blacks to plan or map out career goals. Yet this sort of goal-setting practice seems to be done informally for some whites.

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:
The hiring of women in national staff has been good, but the hiring of blacks is lacking.
There's a distinction between hiring and promotion.... The Post has been good in hiring of minorities but not in promotions.
There's a distinct lack of in-house consultation for blacks and younger women to get over initial hurdles.

White female, Metro, Reporter:
I think more thought should be given to all minorities, not just blacks, as the metropolitan area now has substantial numbers of many diverse groups (Hispanic, East Asians, Muslims) that should be covered.

White female, Editor:
Under its current top newsroom management, this company is not about moving women into supervisory jobs, although this may change as more women move up from middle management. The same goes for black men: As long as they are felt to be capable only up to a certain level, they'll never get ahead. There are some old, long-standing prejudices here that will only change as the generations change. We'll get there, but it will be slow.
There's really no excuse for not having a woman (or black) as AME in the main news operation. Other newspapers have been doing it for years. The mosbach [?] Washington Star had editors (on every desk) of both sexes as far back as the 70s.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Reporter:
Most job prejudice here is more due to cronyism and a preference for Ivy League graduates — take a look at the summer intern lists for the past several years.

White male, Metro, Editor:
We seem to be not as aggressive as other major papers, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the St. Petersburg Times, and many others, in tracking minority candidates from their freshman year in college, staying in touch with them and encouraging the best to come here. Or at least we haven't been doing it as long as the others. The L.A. Times last year brought several editors to a hotel here to meet East Coast minority candidates [brought] here for interviews. Do we do that?
The advancement of blacks here seems to be hampered, as much as anything else, by lack of number of candidates. Once we increase the number, through stronger recruiting, we need to
[continues in right column:]
look at career development. Wouldn't it are [be?] well served having someone concentrate on that, for whites as well as minorities, initiating conversations, seeking goals of employees, reading evaluations, seeing evaluations are done, conferring with department heads, making sure the employee knows what is thought of him and that the company knows where he want to go, and that he knows the likelihood of getting there.
With increasing demands and newsroom priorities in this area, have we checked the size of personnel departments at other major papers to see if the number of people we have on the field at least matches that of our competitors?

White female, National/Financial/Investigations/Foreign, Editor:
I think the questions in this survey woulded [worked?]. In general, I don't believe blacks or other minorities should be hired simply because they are minorities. If all things are more or less equal, then race may enter as a factor in hiring.
I also have not been at The Post long enough and have not been privy to general newsroom information about hiring practices. My initial impression is that women face more subtle barriers than blacks. There is the impression that favoritism is a big factor in advancement. It certainly appears to be true on my desk.

White female, Metro, Reporter:
I feel The Post is going at this the wrong way — how about fellowship assistance to minorities for journalism school coupled with summer jobs? As a "minority" person, I strongly resent the assumption that we need an advocate in the form of a AME. It is insulting!

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Reporter:
The Washington Post Company should be trying to make this a work environment one that would motivate the best reporters, editors, photographers and management from around the country — of all races — to knock down the doors for [a] job. When salary standards compete with the other top two or three newspapers again, this paper's intensified efforts to hire and promote qualified minority candidates should be facilitated.

Black female, Reporter:
I think that The Post is a fine place to work for blacks up to a point, then it appears to me some sort of hidden ceiling beyond which blacks aren't allowed to move, except in the smallest numbers.
I've heard it said second hand that there is a feeling on National/Financial/Inv./Foreign and Foreign that many of the blacks and women who have gone to those staffs "weren't ready." I don't buy it. I think there are a lot of threatened white males who make sure these people don't get the support and assistance their white male peers and friends get and as a result minorities have a much tougher time. You constantly hear stories about the whites on the staffs there undercutting blacks on their beats; telling people not to deal with them. I don't know whether it's true but you hear this a lot.
From my own experience, Metro doesn't have that kind of behavior to the same extent, though I've experienced it. I've actually had people ask me if I could be "objective" about covering blacks; I've had white males I've worked with routinely call women "bitches" and other derogatory names until I've put a stop to it. It demonstrates that we have a ways to go.
Finally, I can't prove it, but my impression is the numbers of blacks on Metro has improved very little under the current regime and that only under great pressure. I don't think there is a commitment to minority hiring'[page ends mid-sentence]

documents.title: Affidavit/declaration of a Post business reporter (paras. 36-45), pages 11-12
documents.subject: First-person written statement in a wage-grievance/arbitration against The Post: retailing/online commerce beat (Apr 2000), airline coverage after Sept. 11, 2001 vs. lower-paid comparator Keith Alexander, second-place press-association award, Knight Foundation fellowship postponed at AME Jill Dutt's request, kidney donation to colleague Warren Brown, book leave (Apr 1 – Aug 1, 2002) for 'Black & White and Red All Over — The Story of a Friendship' (Public Affairs Press), work on the JOBS page from Dec. 1, 2002
documents.date: 2002-2003 (statement covers events through Aug/Dec 2002; drafted shortly after)
documents.notes: Two consecutive typed pages of a numbered-paragraph declaration, page 11 (paras. 36-38) and page 12 (paras. 39-45, text continues past the page break at para. 45). References to AMEs Jill Dutt and Nancy McKeon and Post business-desk events place this in a Washington Post arbitration grievance (likely Martha Hamilton's salary-discrimination case). Narrator covered the retail beat and donated a kidney to Warren Brown; identity not stated on these pages.

pages.transcript:
'36. In April 2000, I applied for and selected to cover the retailing and online commerce beat. On that beat, I was responsible for day to day coverage of general retailing, the grocery industry, consumer products, manufacturers and e-tailing and for larger trend pieces such as the move to 24-7 stores and services and the increase in religious retailing. I also filed stories on breaking news for WashingtonPost.com and provided commentary on News Channel 4 on retailing issues. One of the stories I did was used as the lede in a prototype of a new Sunday Business section that we were planning. It also drew praise from the head of Hechts, Frank Guzzetta, who said he had read everything written about this rival retailer and that my story was the best that had been done.

37. After September 11, 2001, I was called upon to help with the airline industry coverage because of my expertise in that area even though it was not part of my regular beat. I believe that I was being paid less than the person, i.e., Keith Alexander, who was the Post's regular airline industry reporter at the time. Keith was a relatively new Post employee at the time and had substantially less experience than did I. Between Sept. 11 and November 20, when I had surgery, I wrote six front page stories about the airline industry at the same time I continued to cover retailing. Sandra Sugawar [sic, Sugawa] who was directing our airline coverage wrote on Sept. 16: "Len and Larry both told me they love the Friday for Sat story on airports. Len declared it 'great'. I told them you had done a terrific job weaving the different files together. I am hoping it will be okay with Nancy if I use you more when I have these ledealls [sic: lede tails] where files from everyone need to be melded together." This was favorable commentary on my skill in writing a story composed of memos from several reporters in a way that made it seem seamless. Sept. 17, Sugawara e-mailed me: "I told Larry you are doing a fantastic job, and he wants to keep you in the thick of it."

38. I was one of a team of reporters awarded Second Place from the Maryland, Delaware, D.C. Press Association for continuing coverage of the financial aftermath of September 11, 2001.

- 11 -'

'39. In October 2001, I was selected for a Knight Foundation for International Journalism fellowship to go to Mexico to work for six months with young journalists. At the request of AME Jill Dutt, who said she couldn't spare me, I asked the foundation to postpone the fellowship for up to two years.

40. On November 20, 2001 I had surgery. In the weeks leading up to the surgery, I suggested to Nancy McKeon and Jill Dutt that Dina ElBoghdady should begin taking over the retailing beat since I would be recuperating during the key holiday sales season.

41. In the week following surgery, I wrote part of a package for the Washington Post about the surgery in which I donated a kidney to Warren Brown, a colleague in the Financial News Section. It appeared December 11, 2001. This prompted a note from Don Graham which said "Thanks for (among many greater things) one of the best day's [sic] newspaper I've ever seen."

42. When I returned to work in late December 2001, I suggested to Jill Dutt that I continue as a general assignment reporter for a few months. Warren and I had been urged to write a book and were beginning to develop a proposal. I knew that, if we succeeded, I would need additional time off, so it didn't seem fair to start back on the retail beat only to have to drop it again.

43. From April 1, 2002 to August, 2002, I was on leave to write, with Warren Brown a book published by Public Affairs Press: Black & White and Red All Over - The Story of a Friendship. [underlined in original]

44. Upon returning from book leave, I asked to continue covering general assignments for the Business Section because I knew I would be away from work to promote the book. Earlier this month, for instance, Warren and I spent a week in Texas doing book-related appearances.

45. In August, 2002, AME Dutt asked me to edit a new half-page of editorial content to run in the Sunday papers. The page, called the JOBS page, began running on December 1, 2002. documents.title: Arbitration procedures, page 4 (paras. 6-7): counsel, fact-finding conference, witness sequestration, confidentiality of salary information
documents.subject: Typed pages of grievance-arbitration procedural rules: each party may be represented by counsel and is given an opportunity to state its position at the fact-finding conference; witnesses may be sequestered; no party or witness gets name-linked salary/compensation information or performance evaluations of other employees absent a determination of essentiality; confidential information must be available to a party's counsel/representative but not disclosed to third parties
documents.date: unknown (matches the 1997 Settlement Agreement arbitration procedures era)
documents.notes: Single typed page photographed rotated 90° (text reads sideways, top of page at right). Page numbered '- 4 -' at bottom. Terms like 'fact-finding conference' and restrictions on name-linked salary data suggest this is a section of the governing arbitration-procedures document (likely an exhibit to the 1997 WNG/Post Settlement Agreement referenced in DOC-001).

'...may be represented by counsel with other representative[s] of its own choosing.

6. Each party shall be given an opportunity at the beginning of the fact-finding conference to state its position, directly or through counsel or a representative. At the request of either party or on his or her own initiative, the arbitrator may request the presence of witnesses at the fact-finding conference. Witnesses will testify under oath and may be sequestered by the arbitrator. Parties or their counsel or representative may suggest questions to be put to a witness, but all questioning of witnesses shall be by the arbitrator.

7. Under no circumstances shall a claimant or witness be given access to name-linked salary or name-linked compensation information or to performance evaluations of other employees. In addition, other confidential information shall not be disclosed to a party or witness except to the extent that the arbitrator determines that such disclosure of such other confidential information is essential to a fair adjudication of the claim, and that there is no reasonable alternative (including, for example, redaction, preparation of summaries or general descriptions, or the use of compiled or generalized data rather than individualized data).
